summary:
Hungary's civil regime bars transgender people from correcting their legal gender. Administrative refusal became routine from 2018, and the barrier became explicit law in May 2020, when the government legislated by emergency decree during the COVID-19 pandemic to stop passports and identity cards from reflecting an acquired gender, including for people already legally recognised. The same law redefined nem (sex) in the civil code as immutable biological sex. Human Rights Watch records the 2020 provision as banning legal gender change for transgender and intersex people. A trans visitor should expect to enter, be screened and be documented under the marker assigned at birth, with no domestic administrative route to correcting it. Same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since 1961, so the exposure is documentation, recognition and official treatment of the visitor rather than criminal liability for who they are.

A supranational litigation layer runs against that domestic position. On 13 March 2025 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in C-247/23 (Deldits), on a reference from the Budapest High Court in an immigration case, that Article 16 of the GDPR requires the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data once it has changed and no longer complies with the accuracy principle in Article 5(1)(d); the judgment is the operative authority for updating gender markers on official records. In September 2024 a CJEU Advocate General had already called on the Hungarian authorities to correct a transgender refugee's gender marker in the national registries. In April 2026 the Court of Justice found that Orbán-era anti-LGBTQ laws, including the under-18 gender-change ban argued under child-protection law, breached EU rules on several counts, and made an unprecedented finding that Hungary had breached Article 2 of the EU Treaty; the same ruling held that the 2021 child-protection law discriminated against and scapegoated LGBTI residents. That judgment came nine days after the general election.

The political setting changed in April 2026. The 12 April election ended sixteen years of Fidesz rule and returned the Tisza party with 138 seats. Repeal of the anti-LGBTQ laws requires a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly. Budapest Pride's spokesperson, Johanna Majercsik, has named restoration of the right to assembly as the most urgent issue, and Tisza's silence on LGBTQ+ rights under Prime Minister Péter Magyar leaves the pace of change open; commentators describe the election result as a return to a democratic baseline rather than liberation, while rights advocates say they are hopeful that changes will be made. In June 2026 Budapest held its 31st Pride, the first since Viktor Orbán left office, with tens of thousands marching against the backdrop of the laws adopted during his rule. For a visitor, the practical position in mid-2026 is unchanged until repeal legislation actually passes.

Official hostility is documented over more than a decade. In October 2020 Prime Minister Orbán said "gays are to leave our children alone." In May 2020 the National Assembly passed a resolution rejecting the Istanbul Convention, attacking the treaty's measures as promoting "destructive gender ideologies" and "illegal migration." In 2017 Orbán welcomed the World Congress of Families, an organisation designated a hate group by the Southern Poverty Law Center, to the National Parliament. After the Labrisz Lesbian Association published a children's book in 2021, Fidesz ran a campaign conflating homosexuality with paedophilia, and the government-linked outlet Mediaworks published an article calling Labrisz paedophiles without evidence; Labrisz won at first instance, but the Curia ruled in November 2022 that the article did not violate its right to good reputation, and the case was appealed to the Constitutional Court. At Budapest Pride in 2014 the Jobbik party displayed a sign reading "The Parliament Does Not Want Any Deviants" and verbally abused attendees.

Custody and asylum procedures carry their own risks. A 2025 national report by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee and the Háttér Society, produced under an EU-funded project on the rights of LGBTIQ detainees, examines the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in Hungarian detention. In January 2018 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that asylum seekers may not be subjected by authorities to psychological testing aimed at determining sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
Hungary's domestic law sits in open conflict with EU law. The Court of Justice has ruled against the gender-recognition ban and the child-protection law, and C-247/23 (Deldits) supplies a data-protection route to rectifying markers in national registries, yet the ban on legal gender recognition remains in force and no source reviewed shows the government acting on the judgments. Whether a Hungarian authority will apply Deldits to an individual trans person's record is the practical question; the ruling binds the register authority in principle while the domestic statute points the other way.

Repeal depends on arithmetic and political will. The Budapest Pride spokesperson has said the anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds majority, and the incoming government holds 138 seats; some elements are entrenched beyond ordinary legislation, since same-sex marriage was barred by the constitution that took effect on 1 January 2012 and the adoption ban was added by a December 2020 constitutional amendment. The incoming party's priorities on LGBTQ+ rights had not been stated at the time of the sources.
localsOnly:
Registered partnership has been available to same-sex couples since 1 July 2009 and carries the same rights as marriage except adoption, assisted reproduction and the taking of a surname. Unregistered cohabitation has been recognised since 1996 for any couple, including same-sex couples, with specified rights, though inheritance follows only by testament and a widow's pension after ten years. Marriage between people of the same sex was barred by the constitution in force from 1 January 2012.

Because legal gender cannot be corrected and the 2020 redefinition of nem treats sex as immutable biological sex, a transgender resident's relationships are classified against the birth-assigned marker, which determines whether a couple is treated as same-sex or different-sex for these rules. Same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly, stepchild adoption is limited to married different-sex couples, and IVF and donor insemination are unavailable to lesbians in a registered partnership. A December 2020 constitutional amendment banned adoption by same-sex couples and restricted single-parent adoption. In September 2026 Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced an intention to repeal the ban on adoption by same-sex couples.
outOfScopeNotes:
The specific findings of the 2025 Hungarian Helsinki Committee and Háttér Society report on LGBTIQ detainees are not itemised in the sources reviewed. The report's existence and scope are recorded; its conclusions on the treatment of trans detainees in Hungarian custody are unresolved here.

Whether Hungarian authorities are applying the Deldits judgment to individual gender-marker requests is not established by the sources. The ruling binds the register authority in principle, and no source reviewed describes an administrative practice of compliance.

The pace and scope of repeal after April 2026 are unresolved. No repeal legislation had passed at the time of the sources, the incoming government's position on LGBTQ+ rights under Péter Magyar had not been stated, and the Constitutional Court appeal in the Labrisz defamation case had not been decided.
